Question: A 'fleet of agents' is proposed to run production deploys. What governance is non-negotiable?
Option A: More agents increase safety via debate.
Option B: Least-privilege tools, human approval gates on irreversible actions, full traces, and a non-agent rollback path.
Option C: If the planner is staff-level, tools can be root.
Option D: Traces are optional if the model is frontier.

Question: A ReAct-style loop with unbounded “think” tokens before each tool call mainly fails in production because:
Option A: Thoughts are billed, leak into traces, can be injected into, and do not substitute for a real world model
Option B: Thoughts always improve grounding
Option C: Runtimes cannot parse function calls after text
Option D: Stop conditions become stricter automatically

Question: A cost budget that only caps output tokens will still blow up when:
Option A: A tool returns a huge blob that is concatenated into the next prompt every step
Option B: The model emits a short final answer
Option C: You disable retrieval
Option D: You use a state machine with no observations

Question: A state machine whose every node is “LLM decides any tool” has collapsed into free-form. To keep the graph meaningful you must:
Option A: Restrict the tool set and allowed successors per node, with runtime enforcement—not only a prompt that lists them
Option B: Name the nodes poetically
Option C: Increase temperature at terminals
Option D: Remove traces at graph edges

Question: A stop condition “when the model says DONE” is weak because:
Option A: The model can emit DONE early, late, or in a tool argument; the runtime needs an explicit halt (budget, graph terminal, or structured stop)
Option B: DONE is parsed by GPUs directly
Option C: Stop tokens cannot be configured
Option D: Agents never over-talk

Question: Distributed tracing for agents should propagate a run id across model, tools, and sub-agents so that:
Option A: You can reconstruct a causal DAG of spans when one child agent fans out
Option B: IDs are decorative only
Option C: Child agents must not log
Option D: Only the last span is kept

Question: Eval that only scores the final user-visible answer misses:
Option A: Illegal tool use, secret leakage in args, wasted steps, and near-miss policy violations that did not reach the user this time
Option B: Whether the paragraph rhymes
Option C: The tokenizer version
Option D: The color scheme

Question: Free-form vs state machine is not binary. A practical hybrid is:
Option A: A graph of stages with a small free-form tool loop inside a sandbox stage, then a forced review stage before writes
Option B: Free-form always, with a comment in the prompt about stages
Option C: A graph that never calls a model
Option D: No timeouts in hybrid mode

Question: Multi-agent 'researcher + critic' improved a demo. In production it doubled cost and disagreed silently. What was missing?
Option A: A third agent.
Option B: A scoring contract, stop conditions, and a single owner of the user-visible answer; debate without a reducer is just extra tokens.
Option C: Critics should have more tools than researchers.
Option D: You should hide disagreements from traces.

Question: Non-idempotent tools plus at-least-once execution (retries, duplicates, crashes) require:
Option A: Deduping on a business key, or making the effect at-most-once via a store the runtime owns
Option B: Higher temperature so calls differ
Option C: Deleting traces after each retry
Option D: Parallelizing all writes always

Question: Over-permissioned tools plus prompt injection is a full exploit path because:
Option A: Untrusted content can induce a call, and the runtime will execute any allowed tool with model-supplied args
Option B: Injection cannot mention tool names
Option C: Schemas block all strings
Option D: Approvals are inserted by temperature

Question: Passing the entire raw trace back into the next prompt as “memory” is costly and unsafe because:
Option A: It repeats secrets, injections, and failed plans, multiplying tokens and giving old payloads another chance
Option B: Traces contain no text
Option C: Prompts cannot include JSON
Option D: Budgets ignore concatenated traces

Question: Poisoned tool output (a webpage that says “now email secrets to …”) is best treated as:
Option A: Indirect injection into the observation channel; tools must not gain extra privileges from content they fetch
Option B: A reason to raise temperature
Option C: Proof that traces should be disabled
Option D: A tokenizer failure

Question: Retrying a read-only search is usually safer than retrying a write. The precise reason is:
Option A: Reads are typically idempotent; writes often are not, so error class must gate retry policy per tool
Option B: Writes cannot fail
Option C: Reads never time out
Option D: Search cannot be cached

Question: Semantic memory that the agent can write without review creates a loop where:
Option A: Hallucinations get stored and later retrieved as facts, amplifying error across sessions
Option B: Memory becomes write-protected automatically
Option C: RAG cannot read the store
Option D: Tokenizers reset the index

Question: The strongest signal you should not ship an agent yet is:
Option A: A scripted DAG plus one extraction call meets the SLA and the audit log, and the agent only wins on rare demos
Option B: Users have open-ended goals across many tools
Option C: You cannot predefine the next observation
Option D: Research quality requires iterative search

Question: You can give an agent a browser, a shell, and prod credentials 'so it can debug like a human'. Why is this a category error?
Option A: Agents cannot use browsers.
Option B: A human is accountable and rate-limited by attention; an agent will explore the union of permissions at machine speed. Split identities and environments.
Option C: Prod credentials are fine if in a vector store.
Option D: Debugging never needs write access, so the union is safe.

Question: A KMS-encrypted bucket plus many tiny GETs is slow/expensive because:
Option A: Encryption removes copies
Option B: Each request can add KMS authz/decrypt overhead on top of the small-file request tax
Option C: Checksums cannot run with KMS
Option D: SQS cannot send encrypted payloads

Question: A consumer 'succeeds' if it PUTs to S3 but crashes before finishing side effects. Replay will PUT again. The object key should be:
Option A: A random UUID every attempt so nothing clashes
Option B: Deterministic from the message id / business id so retries overwrite the same checksummed object
Option C: The current timestamp to the nanosecond
Option D: The SQS receipt handle

Question: A data lake is 'S3 + many writers renaming prefixes to commit'. Why do staff engineers push for a real table format / manifest?
Option A: Rename is atomic across prefixes in S3 like a filesystem mv of a directory.
Option B: There is no atomic directory rename; readers can see partial sets. Table formats (or a commit inventory) give a consistent snapshot of files.
Option C: S3 LIST is a transaction log.
Option D: Prefix rename is cheaper than writing a manifest.

Question: A pipeline is 'SQS -> worker -> S3 -> notify next queue'. End-to-end exactly-once is:
Option A: Guaranteed by SQS FIFO alone
Option B: Not given; each hop is at-least-once, so idempotent writes (keyed objects/versions) are the real contract
Option C: Guaranteed by S3 copies
Option D: Guaranteed if checksums match

Question: Compare-and-swap with ETags on a hot inventory object serializes the world onto one key. At scale you:
Option A: List the bucket instead
Option B: Shard the object, use a real database for the hot row, or accept queue-based serialization — S3 is not a write-optimized row store
Option C: Turn off checksums to go faster
Option D: Use sequential date prefixes for inventory

Question: Cross-account S3 access: bucket policy vs IAM identity policy vs ACL vs VPC endpoint policy. A request is denied. How do you reason?
Option A: Any one allow wins.
Option B: All relevant layers must allow and none deny; missing identity permission or a VPC endpoint policy deny will fail the call even if the bucket policy allows.
Option C: ACLs override IAM.
Option D: Bucket owner always can, regardless of endpoint policies.

Question: Cross-region replication of S3 objects is asynchronous. Designing a 'read in region B immediately after write in A' as if it were a commit is wrong because:
Option A: Checksums do not replicate
Option B: Replication lag means B may not have the object yet; it is not a distributed database transaction
Option C: Prefixes cannot cross regions
Option D: SQS becomes exactly-once when CRR is on

Question: Durability of copies does not protect you from a bad DELETE in the app. You still need:
Option A: A memorized nines figure
Option B: Versioning, MFA-delete/Object Lock, IAM least privilege, and backups — operational mistakes are not disk failures
Option C: At-most-once SQS so deletes never retry
Option D: Sequential prefixes as undo logs

Question: Firehose/Kinesis rolling files into S3 every N MB or N seconds is about:
Option A: Making S3 a transactional database
Option B: Turning a high-QPS small-event stream into large, checksummed objects with spread prefixes
Option C: Guaranteeing exactly-once SQS
Option D: Avoiding copies for durability

Question: Hot prefix plus small files plus a LIST-heavy UI is a triple hit. The architecture move is:
Option A: Raise the durability SLA
Option B: Metadata in a database or index, objects in S3 with hashed prefixes and batched file sizes; never LIST as the product query
Option C: One SQS message per byte
Option D: Disable checksums and versioning

Question: Inventory reports and S3 Batch exist because listing the live bucket as a control plane:
Option A: Is a strongly consistent SQL view
Option B: Does not scale as a database catalog; you snapshot metadata out of band
Option C: Fixes prefix hotspots
Option D: Makes small files free

Question: S3 Object Lock / WORM helps compliance. Using it as a queue ack store is a smell because:
Option A: WORM objects cannot have checksums
Option B: You wanted a messaging semantic (visibility, retry, DLQ), not immutability of blobs
Option C: Prefixes cannot be locked
Option D: At-least-once is disabled by WORM

Question: Strongly consistent GET of a key is not isolation for a multi-step workflow because:
Option A: Checksums are eventual
Option B: Two objects (or object + queue + table) are not one transaction; you compose idempotent steps
Option C: Prefixes provide SNAPSHOT isolation
Option D: SQS FIFO wraps S3 in a transaction

Question: Using S3 as a lockfile (PUT if not exists, then work) fails under contention because:
Option A: PUT cannot create empty objects
Option B: There is no robust lease/fencing story like a consensus lock; timeouts and retries produce split brain
Option C: Checksums break If-None-Match
Option D: Prefixes serialize all PUTs globally

Question: You are asked to put a POSIX-ish shared scratch filesystem on S3 for a database's data directory. What is the right answer?
Option A: S3 is strongly consistent now, so fsync semantics are met.
Option B: S3 is an object store, not POSIX: no byte-range locking, no real fsync of a mutable file. Use block storage or a real shared FS designed for that DB.
Option C: Mountpoint for S3 is equivalent to ext4 for InnoDB.
Option D: If you enable versioning, POSIX appends work.

Question: You need append-only analytics events. Why not one S3 PUT per click from the browser?
Option A: S3 cannot be written from the internet with the right IAM
Option B: Tiny-object request cost, prefix hotspots, and no server-side aggregation; buffer in Kinesis/SQS/Firehose then write large objects
Option C: Checksums reject click JSON
Option D: At-least-once queues forbid this path only

Question: You replicated objects and now readers see old and new writers. The durable copies did their job; the missing piece is:
Option A: A higher SLA percentage
Option B: An application-level version/epoch so readers know which object generation is authoritative
Option C: Disabling checksums so clocks agree
Option D: Sequential prefixes for linearizability

Question: A key-value API with many overwrite-in-place small rows vs append-mostly events: how do you argue the engine choice?
Option A: In-place small-row OLTP often wants B-tree locality and cheap point/range; append-mostly ingest wants LSM sequential write and later compaction
Option B: Always LSM because write amp is lower in every workload
Option C: Always B-tree because compaction is impossible to operate
Option D: The choice only depends on whether you have a WAL

Question: A leveled compaction write-amp estimate of ~10 (level ratio ~10) is missing which operational multiplier?
Option A: WAL write, memtable flush, and extra L0→L1 work when L0 is unsorted/overlapping
Option B: Bloom-filter hash count
Option C: B-tree fanout
Option D: Replica ping time

Question: A team wants 'just put RocksDB in front of S3' as a global database. What staff-level objection is first?
Option A: RocksDB cannot persist to disk.
Option B: A local LSM is not a distributed consensus/replication layer; you still need sharding, fencing, and a commit protocol or you will split-brain.
Option C: S3 cannot store SSTables.
Option D: Bloom filters do not work outside process memory.

Question: An LSM write stall despite spare CPU often means which resource is the real bottleneck?
Option A: Bloom-filter CPU hash time
Option B: Flush/compaction bandwidth or L0 file-count limits: ingest is gated on making room, not on user-thread CPU
Option C: Too many range-scan merge iterators on idle cores
Option D: The B-tree splitter is running

Question: Delete-heavy LSM with lazy tombstone compaction: what is the dangerous read-path failure mode?
Option A: Point gets return random keys
Option B: Scans and gets keep resurrecting work: they must overlay tombstones from newer files onto older versions until compaction drops them
Option C: The WAL refuses new deletes
Option D: Bloom filters start returning false negatives

Question: Merge iterator during an LSM scan must resolve duplicate keys. What is the correct recency rule?
Option A: Oldest SSTable wins because it was flushed first
Option B: Newest sequence/memtable-or-file generation wins, including tombstones that hide older values
Option C: Largest value wins
Option D: Bloom filters pick the winner

Question: Prefix bloom / partitioned filters exist because of which scan vs get tension?
Option A: Whole-file blooms help point gets but not prefix/range existence checks; partitioned/prefix filters prune files for both
Option B: They replace compaction
Option C: They make SSTables mutable
Option D: They store the full key in RAM

Question: The RUM conjecture is useful when choosing B-tree vs LSM because it says…
Option A: You can independently minimize read, update, and memory/space amplification at once
Option B: You cannot simultaneously minimize read, update, and memory/space amplification; LSM and B-tree sit on different corners
Option C: Only RAM size matters; on-disk layout is irrelevant
Option D: Compaction eliminates all three amplifications

Question: Tombstones in an LSM outlive the data they delete under a bad compaction policy. How do reads fail?
Option A: They don't; tombstones are skipped in O(1).
Option B: Point and especially range reads must sift dead keys until compaction drops them; space and CPU inflate.
Option C: Tombstones automatically promote to the memtable as live keys.
Option D: The WAL refuses new writes until tombstones are gone.

Question: Why can a copy-on-write B-tree (or CoW page engine) still lose the LSM ingest race under random writes?
Option A: CoW still tends to write page-granularity trees and can amplify through ancestors; LSM batches into sequential runs
Option B: CoW never writes a WAL
Option C: CoW cannot be crash-safe
Option D: LSM never writes more than once

Question: Why is fsync of the WAL not the same as fsync of SSTables for crash correctness?
Option A: WAL fsync makes the latest memtable mutations recoverable; SSTable fsync makes a flush durable so WAL can be truncated
Option B: Only SSTable fsync matters; WAL is a cache
Option C: Only WAL fsync matters; SSTables can be torn forever
Option D: Both are optional if bloom filters are used

Question: Why is naive size-tiered compaction prone to space-amp spikes right before a large merge?
Option A: A merge of similar-sized runs temporarily keeps old and new copies until the new file is installed
Option B: Bloom filters double on disk
Option C: The WAL is checkpointed into every SSTable twice
Option D: Memtables are never released

Question: You are picking a storage engine for a write-heavy metrics store with occasional large range scans for graphs. What is the real tension?
Option A: LSM ingest vs the merge cost of those range scans (and compaction stealing I/O from queries).
Option B: B-trees cannot store timestamps.
Option C: LSMs cannot expire old data.
Option D: Range scans are always O(1) on both.

Question: You have a block cache that already holds most inner index blocks. Where should you spend the next RAM dollar for LSM point gets?
Option A: Always more bloom-filter bits, even if data blocks are never cached
Option B: It depends: blooms cut negative lookups; caching data/filter blocks cuts positive lookups. Measure miss types
Option C: Never bloom filters if any cache exists
Option D: Always enlarge the WAL

Question: You must pick a structure for a working set that fits in RAM but a dataset that does not. Which statement is the staff-level read of amplification?
Option A: If internal nodes/filters/hot leaves stay cached, B-tree point reads can be one I/O; LSM still pays multi-level filter/index misses on cold keys
Option B: RAM size makes on-disk layout irrelevant
Option C: LSM point reads become free because memtable holds the dataset
Option D: Write amplification disappears when the working set is cached

Question: You observe LSM read amp rising while write amp falls after switching compaction style. What did you likely just do?
Option A: Moved toward more aggressive leveling (more rewrite, fewer overlapping files)
Option B: Moved toward lazier tiered/universal merging (less rewrite, more overlapping runs)
Option C: Disabled the WAL
Option D: Replaced blooms with a full in-memory index of every key

Question: A low-latency path allocates on every message (std::string, vector resize). The profiler is 'clean' of locks. What is still wrong?
Option A: Allocators are wait-free and never stall.
Option B: Allocator contention and cache pollution; pre-size, arenas, or intrusive buffers belong on that path.
Option C: The compiler elides all heap use in loops.
Option D: virtual functions are the only latency bug that matters.

Question: A sanitizer-clean binary still corrupts state only at -O3. What class of bug is first on the list?
Option A: A missing #include.
Option B: Undefined behavior the optimizer exploited (strict aliasing, signed overflow, lifetime) that -O0 happened not to.
Option C: The linker strips atomics at -O3.
Option D: Sanitizers prove the absence of UB at all optimization levels.

Question: A tight packet loop uses virtual dispatch per packet on a deep hierarchy. Profile shows i-cache misses. What is the data-oriented move?
Option A: Add more virtual methods to improve prediction.
Option B: Sort by type, use a closed set of concrete handlers, or a table of function pointers over contiguous data — cut the pointer chase.
Option C: virtual is always inlined by LTO.
Option D: Put each packet on its own heap allocation for locality.

Question: An ABI-stable plugin interface returns `std::string` across a `.so` boundary compiled with different libstdc++. What did you just do?
Option A: The Itanium ABI makes all std::string layouts identical forever.
Option B: You invoked ODR/ABI roulette: layout and allocators may differ; use a C ABI (char* + length) or a single shared standard library.
Option C: unique_ptr across .so is always safe if string is not.
Option D: C++ modules fix ABI at the filesystem boundary.

Question: You must keep ABI stable for a C++ library used by customers' compilers. Which surface is the least painful?
Option A: Inline templates and std::string in the public API.
Option B: A C API (opaque handles, explicit sizes) with C++ wrappers in a header that the customer compiles.
Option C: Exporting std::vector from a .so compiled with a different libstdc++.
Option D: Throwing exceptions across the .so boundary as the stable contract.

Question: You need to share read-mostly config across threads. A shared_ptr swapped atomically vs a mutex around a unique_ptr. What is the RCU-like idea?
Option A: Mutex is always lower latency for reads.
Option B: Publish a new immutable snapshot (atomic shared_ptr); readers copy the pointer with no lock; old snapshot frees when refcount hits 0.
Option C: unique_ptr can be read from two threads if it is const.
Option D: atomics on unique_ptr are in the standard and cheaper.

Question: You need wait-free reads of a config blob. Writers are rare. Which pattern matches?
Option A: A single mutex around a unique_ptr that readers also take.
Option B: Immutable snapshots published with atomic shared_ptr (or RCU); readers load the pointer, writers publish a new object.
Option C: volatile on the unique_ptr.
Option D: memory_order_relaxed stores of a mutex.

Question: A coordinator chooses replicas for a QUORUM read. Why might it still do extra digest reads?
Option A: To hash the partition key again
Option B: To detect replica disagreement cheaply, then fetch full data and reconcile, which is a form of read repair work
Option C: Digest reads replace QUORUM
Option D: Digests are only for hinted handoff

Question: A globally distributed Cassandra app uses LOCAL_QUORUM in each DC and never repairs. What consistency story are you actually giving users who travel between DCs?
Option A: Linearizable global reads.
Option B: A DC-local quorum that can remain stale vs another DC until repair/hint/read-repair; design for it or use a different consistency/replication model.
Option C: LOCAL_QUORUM waits for all DCs.
Option D: Hinted handoff makes DCs interchangeable immediately.

Question: A repair that misses a recently deleted partition (gc grace elapsed, tombstone dropped, replica was down) produces what?
Option A: A harmless no-op
Option B: Data resurrection: the stale replica's live data is copied back to others
Option C: Automatic RF increase
Option D: LWT abort of the repair

Question: A staff review of a 'one partition per tenant, all rows clustered' multi-tenant design should flag what first?
Option A: CQL cannot filter clustering columns
Option B: Tenant size skew becomes hot/wide partitions; noisy tenants dominate compaction, repair, and replica CPU with no token isolation
Option C: RF cannot be greater than 1 for multi-tenant data
Option D: QUORUM does not work with clustering columns

Question: Compaction strategy: STCS on a time-series table that mostly appends and TTLs. Why might TWCS be the better fit?
Option A: STCS is illegal on time-series.
Option B: Time-window compaction can drop whole SSTables when TTL expires instead of mixing old/new in size-tiered compaction, reducing tombstone pain.
Option C: TWCS makes all reads QUORUM.
Option D: TWCS stores data in B-trees.

Question: Dropping gc_grace to 'clean tombstones faster' after a mass delete: what must already be true?
Option A: Nothing; it is always safe
Option B: Every replica has received the deletes and repair has covered the ranges; otherwise dropped tombstones invite resurrection
Option C: CL=ONE is in use
Option D: LWTs are disabled

Question: Hinted handoff during a rolling outage of two of three replicas at RF=3, CL=QUORUM: what happens to writes?
Option A: Writes succeed because hints count as quorum votes
Option B: QUORUM writes fail; hints are not a substitute for live acknowledgements, so availability drops until a replica returns
Option C: CL is automatically lowered to ONE
Option D: The remaining replica becomes RF=1 silently

Question: Hot-partition mitigation via bucketing (user_id + bucket) changes which costs?
Option A: It removes the need for RF
Option B: Writes spread across tokens, but reads of 'all buckets' become scatter-gather and you reintroduce merge/limit logic in the app
Option C: Clustering order is lost forever
Option D: QUORUM is no longer defined

Question: Incremental repair vs a naive full repair: what failure mode are you trying to avoid?
Option A: Token-aware routing
Option B: Repeatedly streaming already-agreed ranges, overloading disks/network, and extending the window where unrepaired data can resurrect after tombstone GC
Option C: The need for partition keys
Option D: Use of clustering columns

Question: LWT cost is not just extra round trips. What local storage-engine cost also shows up?
Option A: Paxos state (promises/commits) is persisted per partition, adding writes, contention, and more compaction on that key
Option B: LWT bypasses memtables entirely
Option C: LWT stores a full cluster snapshot
Option D: LWT turns off bloom filters cluster-wide

Question: W+R>RF is necessary but not sufficient for 'I always read my write' in Cassandra. Which extra caveat is staff-level?
Option A: There are no caveats if W+R>RF
Option B: Clock/last-write-wins, partial replica failures, digest mismatch paths, and CL computed per-DC can still yield surprising recency without LWT/SERIAL
Option C: Partition keys are not hashed when W+R>RF
Option D: Tombstones disable W+R>RF

Question: When would you accept CL=ONE writes in production despite stale-read risk?
Option A: Always; QUORUM is never worth it
Option B: When the workload is write-availability-first, reads can tolerate staleness, and repair/hints/read-repair are operated as the reconciliation path
Option C: When you also need linearizable CAS
Option D: When RF=1 already, so CL does not matter and you still claim multi-replica durability

Question: Why can EACH_QUORUM writes be the right multi-DC choice even though they are slow?
Option A: They contact only one node
Option B: They require a quorum in every DC, so a DC that was partitioned does not silently accept a CL that later cannot be read locally
Option C: They skip the commit log
Option D: They disable tombstones

Question: Why is a monotonically growing clustering key that is also the only partition key a dual foot-gun?
Option A: It is the recommended time-series pattern
Option B: One ever-growing partition (hot + wide) lands on one token; time-series wants time in clustering and a bounded partition key (and often time buckets)
Option C: Clustering keys cannot be timestamps
Option D: QUORUM forbids time-series

Question: You must explain why Cassandra's last-write-wins on conflicting replicas is not a substitute for LWT.
Option A: LWW always waits for Paxos
Option B: LWW picks a timestamp winner after the fact; concurrent RMWs can lose updates. LWT prevents the lost update by agreeing before commit
Option C: LWW and LWT are identical on the same partition
Option D: Repair turns LWW into linearizability

Question: You need a uniqueness constraint ('this email is registered') in Cassandra. Why is that a product smell at staff level?
Option A: Cassandra unique indexes are serializable by default.
Option B: Uniqueness is a consensus problem; LWT per email works at modest QPS and becomes a hotspot/latency tax. Often the source of truth belongs in a database that does this cheaply.
Option C: A secondary index on email is unique automatically.
Option D: Partitioning on email hashes uniqueness for free.

Question: You need linearizable compare-and-set on a counter-like row. Why is 'read QUORUM then write QUORUM' the wrong tool?
Option A: QUORUM cannot read counters
Option B: Two clients can both read the same value and both write; you need LWT/Paxos (or an external consensus) to serialize the RMW
Option C: Repair already serializes all writes
Option D: Hinted handoff provides linearizability

Question: A 'linked list of buffers' vs a small number of large slabs for a network server. Same abstract list of bytes. Why slabs?
Option A: Fewer allocations, sequential DMA/cache, cheaper to coalesce; the pointer-rich list maximizes syscall and miss cost per byte
Option B: The kernel can only send linked lists
Option C: Slabs cannot represent a queue
Option D: BFS requires one malloc per byte

Question: A rate limiter for a global API: token bucket in one Redis vs sliding log of timestamps per user. What is the staff trade-off?
Option A: They are identical at all scales.
Option B: Token bucket is O(1) memory/CPU and approximate; a precise sliding log is memory-heavy per key and harder to shard. Pick based on fairness vs cost.
Option C: Sliding log is O(1) and token bucket is O(n).
Option D: Only a bloom filter can rate-limit correctly.

Question: Autocomplete at 50k QPS: trie in one JVM vs prefix query to a search engine. When is the trie the wrong 'clever' answer?
Option A: Tries are always smaller than inverted indexes.
Option B: When the dictionary is huge, needs fuzzy/ranked results, or must be updated without STW rebuilds — operational cost dominates Big-O.
Option C: Search engines cannot do prefix match.
Option D: A trie cannot be sharded.

Question: CHAMP / HAMT / B-tree vs open-addressing hash for a persistent (immutable) map in a language runtime. Why the tree-like hash trie?
Option A: Structural sharing on update: you copy a path, not the whole table — a flat hash array maps poorly onto persistent workloads even if lookups are similar
Option B: Trees cannot share structure
Option C: Open addressing is required for immutability
Option D: Heaps persist better because extract-min copies nothing

Question: Counting Bloom / cuckoo / quotient filters exist. You need deletes and a hard bound on false positives for a security denylist. Why a vanilla Bloom is the wrong contract?
Option A: Standard Bloom cannot delete safely and never gives 0% false positives — a 'yes' could allow or deny the wrong principal; use an exact set or a structure with bounded, understood errors
Option B: Vanilla Bloom has false negatives, which are worse for denylists
Option C: Union-find can delete Bloom bits
Option D: LRU turns Bloom into an exact set

Question: Dijkstra on a huge sparse graph: binary heap vs array vs Fibonacci-style vs just BFS. Workload split?
Option A: If all weights are equal, BFS (or 0-1 deque) — a heap is wasted. If weights vary, you need a PQ; which PQ depends on decrease-key volume and graph size, not the brand name
Option B: Always Fibonacci heap because the bound is famous
Option C: DFS with a Bloom filter replaces Dijkstra
Option D: Union-find extracts the next closest node

Question: Directed graph, detect if adding an edge would create a cycle, online, many queries. DFS every time is too slow. Better?
Option A: If the graph is a DAG of components you merge, union-find works for undirected; for directed you need incremental topo / reachability (or full topo + DFS on the relevant region) — union-find alone is the wrong connectivity model
Option B: Union-find is identical for directed cycles
Option C: A Bloom filter of edges proves acyclicity
Option D: BFS from a random node never sees directed cycles

Question: False-positive rate of a Bloom filter after you insert more items than it was sized for. What actually happens?
Option A: Bits saturate, 'yes' becomes almost always — the filter silently degrades toward useless; there is no crash, which is why ops miss it
Option B: It starts emitting false negatives to compensate
Option C: Union-find rebuilds the bitset
Option D: LRU evicts bits in recency order

Question: Hot-key workload: 1 key is 40% of QPS. Hash partition across 50 caches. What structure-level fact did you ignore?

Question: LRU under scan-heavy traffic (a job reads every key once). What happens to the cache of hot keys?

Question: Rendezvous hashing vs consistent ring: you want minimal disruption and easy weighted nodes without virtual node explosion. Which idea?

Question: You external-sort huge files. Runs are written, then merged. Why does 'stable' still matter on disk?

Question: You need an LRU across a fleet. Local LRU per node + consistent hashing. A key's node jumps; the new node has a cold LRU. Besides miss storm, what invariant broke?

Question: A 350KB item is updated 20 times a second to flip one flag. Why is this an incident waiting to happen?

Question: Adaptive capacity moved extra throughput toward a hot partition, but p99 still collapses on one productId. What is left?

Option C: Gap locks are omitted from redo
Option D: Covering indexes become invalid on replicas

Question: You observe replication lag that grows only when the primary does bulk LOAD. Row-based replication is on. Why can the replica still fall over?
Option A: Row-based events for huge writes apply row-by-row on the replica, often without the primary's bulk optimizations.
Option B: Replicas ignore LOAD DATA.
Option C: Binlog compresses bulk loads to one page the replica cannot unpack.
Option D: The replica must take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on every table.

Question: You set replica_preserve_commit_order = ON with parallel workers. Throughput drops vs unordered apply. Why is that the correct default for many systems?
Option A: Readers and cascading replicas observe the same commit order as the source, avoiding anomalies that cheaper parallel apply would allow
Option B: Commit order preservation disables the redo log on the replica
Option C: It is required for covering indexes to work
Option D: It prevents gap locks on the source

Question: You split a hotspot table by hash of tenant_id into multiple tables to reduce clustered-page contention. Which cost did you just accept?
Option A: Cross-tenant queries, FKs, and online DDL become N-way operations; replication parallelism may improve only if transactions do not touch many shards
Option B: InnoDB can no longer use secondary indexes
Option C: Gap locks disappear because hash tables have no order
Option D: The buffer pool cannot cache more than one shard

Question: temp tables in a transaction with binlog ROW and a rollback. Why can disk and replication still surprise you?
Option A: Some temp-table patterns still write row events or consume undo/ibtmp; rollback does not shrink files, and mixed temp usage can desync replicas if logged incorrectly
Option B: Temporary tables are always replicated as CREATE TABLE on disk
Option C: Rollback of temp tables requires a full clustered rebuild of user tables
Option D: Gap locks on temp tables are copied to the replica

Question: A BRIN index is chosen for a time-series table that is updated in the middle of the key range. Why does BRIN degrade?
Option A: BRIN summarizes page ranges; random updates destroy correlation so range summaries become too wide to prune
Option B: BRIN cannot coexist with WAL
Option C: BRIN requires SERIALIZABLE to return correct results
Option D: BRIN stores one pointer per tuple like btree

Question: A connection pooler in session mode plus thousands of idle-in-transaction sessions. Memory on the database host climbs. Why is this worse than idle (not in transaction)?
Option A: Each idle-in-transaction backend holds a snapshot, preventing xmin advancement, vacuum, and releasing of catalog caches tied to that snapshot
Option B: Idle-in-transaction sessions do not use a backend process
Option C: PostgreSQL automatically sets synchronous_commit = off for idle transactions
Option D: WAL is fsynced continuously for idle snapshots

Question: A multi-master-like design uses logical replication with conflict avoidance by partitioning key ranges per node. An UPDATE moves a row across ranges. What breaks?
Option A: The UPDATE is not a DELETE+INSERT across publications, so the row can vanish or duplicate depending on replica identity and filters
Option B: PostgreSQL converts the UPDATE into a HOT update on the subscriber automatically
Option C: WAL is not generated for cross-range updates
Option D: synchronous_commit ignores logical slots for such rows

Question: A multi-tenant SaaS puts all tenants in one cluster. One tenant runs analytical queries that blow up work_mem and temp files. What isolation strategy actually protects neighbors?
Option A: A single `statement_timeout` equal for everyone is enough.
Option B: Separate roles/pools with memory/timeouts, plus (if needed) separate databases or clusters; Postgres does not give hard multi-tenant CPU isolation inside one instance.
Option C: MVCC isolates CPU as well as row versions.
Option D: Put the noisy tenant on a replica and they cannot affect the primary's CPU.

Question: A partial index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL becomes huge despite few live rows. What went wrong?
Option A: Updates that set deleted_at still leave index entries for old MVCC versions until vacuum; a long xmin horizon prevents cleanup
Option B: Partial indexes index every row regardless of predicate
Option C: IS NULL predicates cannot be used in partial indexes
Option D: HOT updates duplicate partial index entries on purpose

Question: A query uses a GiST index on a range type. Concurrent updates cause a lot of page splits. Which correctness vs performance tension exists?
Option A: GiST must maintain balanced predicate trees under MVCC, so splits WAL-log internal pages and can bloat faster than btree on overlapping ranges
Option B: GiST updates are never WAL-logged, risking replica divergence
Option C: GiST ignores isolation levels by design
Option D: VACUUM cannot recycle GiST pages without REINDEX CONCURRENTLY plus a restart

Question: A standby is used for read scaling. A long reporting query on the standby conflicts with WAL replay of a VACUUM that wants to remove tuples still visible to the query. What happens if hot_standby_feedback is off and max_standby_streaming_delay is short?
Option A: The standby cancels the query so replay can proceed, or replay waits then cancels—reads are sacrificed to keep apply moving
Option B: The primary automatically delays VACUUM until the standby query ends, with no configuration
Option C: The standby silently returns wrong results for removed tuples
Option D: HOT chains are rebuilt on the standby without canceling queries

Question: Connection poolers (PgBouncer) in transaction pooling hide session state. Which app pattern silently breaks?
Option A: Simple prepared statements that last one transaction.
Option B: Session-level features: SET, temp tables, WITH HOLD cursors, advisory locks you expected to last the HTTP connection.
Option C: Read-only queries.
Option D: Using a single user role.

Question: During a crash recovery, redo is slow because of a huge uncheckpointed WAL volume after a bulk load with few checkpoints. What is the trade-off you mis-set?
Option A: High max_wal_size / checkpoint_timeout reduced checkpoint I/O during the load but lengthened crash recovery
Option B: synchronous_commit = off disables redo entirely
Option C: full_page_writes = on prevents recovery from using WAL
Option D: HOT updates cannot be redone, so recovery rebuilds indexes from scratch

Question: Hash partitioning vs range partitioning for a multi-tenant id. Queries always filter by tenant_id. Why might hash still be the wrong choice at staff scale?
Option A: You cannot drop a tenant by detaching one partition; data for one tenant is scattered, so retention and locality suffer
Option B: Hash partitions cannot have indexes
Option C: The planner cannot prune hash partitions even with equality on the partition key
Option D: HOT updates are impossible on hash partitions

Question: On a huge append-only table, aggressive autovacuum still scans endlessly. What freeze/visibility-map strategy actually reduces that work?
Option A: Insert-only vacuum and freezing new pages so the visibility map stays all-visible and future vacuums skip them
Option B: Disable freeze because append-only tables never wrap XIDs
Option C: Create more btree indexes so vacuum can skip the heap
Option D: Set synchronous_commit = off to skip freezing

Question: Synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ: commits now wait on the network. A failover-happy load balancer flaps the standby. What failure did you couple into the write path?
Option A: None; sync replica loss is ignored until you promote.
Option B: Commits stall or fail when the sync standby is unhealthy; you bought durability/availability of the standby into every write's latency SLO.
Option C: PostgreSQL automatically falls back to local commits with the same RPO.
Option D: The primary buffers sync commits in shared buffers indefinitely.

Question: You are choosing between a huge partitioned table with a global unique constraint vs uniqueness in the application. PostgreSQL unique indexes are per partition (unless you include the partition key). What is the real design constraint?
Option A: Global uniqueness is free if you use logical replication.
Option B: A unique index can only guarantee uniqueness within the index's scope; cross-partition uniqueness needs the partition key in the constraint or an external allocator.
Option C: Partitioning always preserves all unique constraints of the parent with no extra columns.
Option D: Unique constraints are enforced by WAL, which is global.

Question: You enable checksums after seeing silent corruption on a replica. What operational cost is now permanent?
Option A: Every heap/index page read verifies checksums and writes pay to maintain them, adding CPU; enabling later still requires a rewrite of all files
Option B: Checksums replace WAL, so crash recovery is skipped
Option C: Checksums only apply when synchronous_commit is off
Option D: MVCC visibility is stored in checksums instead of hint bits

Question: You need close-to-zero downtime DDL on a 10 TB table (add a column with a non-constant default, historically). What is the staff-level instinct?
Option A: Run it in a transaction on the primary during peak; MVCC makes it instant.
Option B: Treat it as an expand/contract migration: add nullable column, backfill in batches, then constrain — not one blocking rewrite if the version still rewrites.
Option C: Logical replication ignores table rewrites, so just ALTER.
Option D: Global indexes make any DDL O(1).

Question: You need zero-downtime DDL that rewrites a table (type change). Why is CREATE TABLE new + concurrent backfill + swap still hard in PostgreSQL?
Option A: In-flight writes, identity/serial sequences, FK/triggers, and logical replica identity must be dual-written or locked around cutover or rows are lost
Option B: PostgreSQL cannot CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the new table
Option C: MVCC prevents INSERT into two tables in one transaction
Option D: WAL cannot contain both old and new row formats

Question: You observe subtransaction overflow (pg_subtrans) under a PL/pgSQL loop of SAVEPOINTs. What is the failure mode?
Option A: Hint-bit and snapshot checks degrade because subxids no longer fit in the in-memory cache, causing pg_subtrans I/O
Option B: WAL is discarded for nested subtransactions
Option C: HOT updates are forced for every SAVEPOINT
Option D: The backend switches isolation to READ UNCOMMITTED

Question: full_page_writes is on (default). After a checkpoint, the first change to a page writes a full page image. How does this interact with a storage that already does atomic 8K writes?
Option A: You still pay WAL amplification to protect against torn pages on typical hardware; turning it off is only safe on systems that guarantee atomic page writes
Option B: full_page_writes is redundant with MVCC and can always be off
Option C: full_page_writes only applies to indexes, not heap
Option D: Replicas ignore full page images and reconstruct pages from btree

Question: hot_standby_feedback = on protects standby queries from replay conflict. What cost does the primary pay?
Option A: Vacuum on the primary cannot remove tuples still needed by standby snapshots, so bloat and wraparound risk grow with long standby queries
Option B: The primary disables HOT updates
Option C: synchronous_commit is forced to remote_apply
Option D: Indexes on the primary cannot be used until feedback ACKs

Question: A data pipeline pickles pandas objects between steps. After a pandas upgrade, workers cannot read old files. What was the architectural mistake?
Option A: pandas objects cannot be serialized.
Option B: Pickle is an in-process, version-fragile format; a durable pipeline wants parquet/arrow/json with a schema.
Option C: You should have used `eval`.
Option D: Pickle is schema-stable across pandas majors.

Question: A native C extension allocates GIL-holding work for 50ms per request. How do you get concurrency back?
Option A: Add more threads; the GIL will schedule them during the 50ms.
Option B: Release the GIL in the extension around the heavy work, or move it out of process; otherwise threads buy nothing.
Option C: asyncio.wait will interleave C code.
Option D: Set `PYTHONTHREADSAWARE=1`.

Question: A scientific team wants to run a 32-core CPU-bound pipeline in one CPython process with threads. What do you change in the architecture?
Option A: Increase thread count to 256.
Option B: Use processes, a native GIL-releasing library, or another runtime; threads will not use the cores for bytecode.
Option C: Enable asyncio; it bypasses the GIL for CPU.
Option D: The GIL is gone for CPU loops if you `await` them.

Question: A web worker pool + a background thread that mutates a dict without locks. GIL makes this 'safe', right?
Option A: Yes; GIL serializes all bytecode so dicts are atomic for any compound update.
Option B: No; GIL can interleave bytecode between operations; dict compound updates still need locks or a queue to a single owner thread.
Option C: dicts are immutable in CPython.
Option D: Only list.append needs a lock.

Question: Subinterpreters / free-threading are on the table. What still has to be true of your C extensions?
Option A: They are automatically safe because they used the GIL once.
Option B: They must be explicit about shared state; many extensions still assume a single interpreter and a GIL.
Option C: All PyPI wheels are already free-threaded.
Option D: Only the stdlib needs changes; extensions cannot share objects.

Question: You must hot-reload code in a long-lived worker. Why is `importlib.reload` a staff-level last resort?
Option A: reload cannot fail.
Option B: Old objects, class identities, and singletons survive; you get mixed versions and leaking modules. Prefer rolling new processes.
Option C: reload is the same as restarting the interpreter.
Option D: CPython forbids reload in production by raising.

Question: You must ship a tool to air-gapped machines. What packaging failure mode should you design against?
Option A: wheels always contain every manylinux ABI.
Option B: Native deps, implicit system libraries, and 'pip install from PyPI' at runtime; vendoring/lock a compatible wheel set or use a frozen runtime.
Option C: CPython binaries are identical across distros.
Option D: venv is guaranteed present on all OS images.

Question: A 'Redis transaction' across keys in different slots needs:
Option A: MULTI/EXEC only
Option B: A different design: hash tags to colocate, an external workflow, or a real database transaction — Cluster will refuse the cross-slot MULTI
Option C: RDB snapshot isolation
Option D: Pub/Sub as the commit log

Question: A cluster slot migration is in progress. Clients must handle:
Option A: A frozen keyspace with no errors
Option B: ASK/MOVED redirects and transient multi-key failures; treating Redis like a single always-local node will break
Option C: Automatic AOF merge across nodes
Option D: Synchronous replica promotion of every key

Question: A platform team offers Redis as 'multi-tenant durable storage' with one cluster and no key namespaces/limits. What will happen?
Option A: Redis ACLs make noisy neighbors impossible.
Option B: One tenant's large keys, KEYS, or unbounded growth will stall or evict everyone; you need isolation (instances), maxmemory policies, and key prefixes with hard quotas.
Option C: Cluster slots isolate tenants automatically.
Option D: AOF rewrite is per key, so tenants cannot interact.

Question: AOF rewrite and RDB fork at the same time on a memory-tight host. Operational risk?
Option A: Slots reshuffle
Option B: Double copy-on-write memory spike, latency stall, or OOM killer — persistence settings are a capacity plan, not just 'on'
Option C: Eviction turns into noeviction
Option D: Replicas become source of truth

Question: Big keys (a million-member hash) hurt more than memory size because:
Option A: Cluster cannot hash them
Option B: Many commands become O(N) on the single thread (serialize, expire, replica sync, client output)
Option C: AOF cannot log hashes
Option D: Eviction skips hashes

Question: Blocking commands (BLPOP, BZPOPMIN) on a shared instance interact with the single thread how?
Option A: They run on a second GIL
Option B: They park that client, but a flood of them plus large fanout still competes for the one command loop and output buffers
Option C: They force AOF off
Option D: They rebalance slots

Question: Client-side caching / tracking exists because:
Option A: The server thread wants more KEYS calls
Option B: Even an in-memory round trip is expensive at huge QPS; local memory with invalidation beats a hot Redis key
Option C: AOF becomes optional then
Option D: Slots move to the client

Question: Hash-slot coverage after a node death: the cluster goes down for those slots unless:
Option A: AOF is always fsynced
Option B: Replicas exist for that node and failover succeeds; Redis Cluster is not magic extra durability of the data model
Option C: Eviction is LRU
Option D: Clients retry KEYS

Question: Redis is used as a session store. A replica is promoted after async replication lag. What did users just lose, and what is the staff fix?
Option A: Nothing; promotion waits for replicas.
Option B: Recent sessions/writes that never made the replica; either accept RPO, use WAIT/sync replication (latency), or don't put irreplaceable sessions only in Redis.
Option C: AOF on the new primary contains the old primary's unsent writes automatically.
Option D: Clients reconnect and Redis heals sessions from S3.

Question: Serving cache-aside correctly means on write you:
Option A: Only SET Redis and trust eviction to notify the DB
Option B: Write the database first (or in a defined order) and invalidate/update Redis so the cache cannot resurrect stale truth
Option C: KEYS and rewrite all entries
Option D: Disable TTL so Redis becomes source of truth

Question: Stampede plus a single-threaded Redis plus a slow DB fill is a cascade. A robust refill looks like:
Option A: TTL=0 on every key
Option B: One owner refills, others wait or serve stale; optionally jitter TTLs; never let N app servers all reconstruct the same key
Option C: Flushall on miss
Option D: Disable pipelining during refill

Question: Streams with consumer groups beat a naive list queue when:
Option A: You need cluster-wide ACID
Option B: You need pending entries, acknowledgements, and replay after a worker crash — still not a durable business ledger by itself
Option C: You need strongly consistent GSIs
Option D: You want eviction to delete jobs first

Question: WAIT or WAITAOF after a write is how you:
Option A: Make Redis a multi-primary consensus store
Option B: Block until replicas (or AOF) catch up to a durability bar you chose; default writes do not wait
Option C: Disable eviction globally
Option D: Rebalance slots

Question: Why can pipelining + Cluster be wrong if you blindly batch keys?
Option A: Pipelines cannot send SET
Option B: A pipeline is still per-node; mixed slots must be split by slot or you get CROSSSLOT / extra hops
Option C: Pipelines force RDB
Option D: Pipelines disable eviction mid-batch as a transaction

Question: Why still persist a write to Postgres (or similar) when Redis already SET it?
Option A: Postgres is faster
Option B: Redis may evict, lose a replica, or replay an older RDB; the database is the source of truth, Redis is a copy
Option C: Cluster slots require SQL
Option D: AOF cannot store the same string

Question: You need a distributed lock. Someone uses SET NX without expiry, or with expiry but no fencing token. What bug remains?
Option A: None; NX is a correct lock.
Option B: A lock can be held forever, or expire while work continues and a second worker runs — without fencing, both sides mutate the resource.
Option C: Redis locks are linearizable if you use WAIT.
Option D: Expiry is unnecessary if clients are in the same VPC.

Question: You observe p99 spikes every N minutes with no app deploy. A likely Redis cause is:
Option A: Cluster slots wrapping at 16384
Option B: Fork-based persistence, large expiry storms, or big-key commands — all block or stall the same thread
Option C: Eventually consistent reads
Option D: On-demand memory billing

Question: A payment service must not lose 'charge then record' if the process dies after HTTP 200 from Stripe. What Spring-centric pattern actually works?
Option A: @Transactional around the Stripe SDK call.
Option B: Idempotency key + outbox (record intent, commit, then charge/publish) so crash recovery can finish the work without double-charge.
Option C: @Async so the charge happens after response.
Option D: XA with Stripe's JDBC driver.

Question: Two Boot services share a database and Hibernate entities. Why do staff platform teams fight this?
Option A: Hibernate cannot map the same table twice in the world.
Option B: You coupled deployability and schemas: migrations, locks, and incompatible entity changes become a distributed monolith. Split data ownership.
Option C: Spring forbids two apps on one JDBC URL.
Option D: Connection pools cannot be sized per service.

Question: You inherited a monolith Boot app that starts a full context for every integration test. CI is 40 minutes. What is the staff testing strategy?
Option A: Only @SpringBootTest; slicing hides bugs.
Option B: Slice tests for web/data, testcontainers for a few contract tests, and a small number of full-context smoke tests — not a full boot per method.
Option C: Disable tests in CI to restore speed.
Option D: Replace JUnit with main() methods.
